papers.what_it_is: A six-page survey and small re-implementation study of classical and quantum recurrent and self-attention sequence models (QRNN, QSANN), with a positional-encoding addition to QSANN, tested on small text and image tasks.

assertions.value: The authors state that their objective is a brief survey of classical and quantum neural-net sequence models, with a focus on recent quantum approaches proposed to work with near-term quantum devices.
quotes: Our primary objective is to conduct a brief survey of various classical and quantum neural net sequence models
with a focus on recent quantum approaches proposed to work with near-term quantum devices
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract states the paper's own scope.

assertions.value: The authors state that they re-implemented a representative set of existing methods, adapted an image-classification approach using quantum self-attention into a quantum hybrid transformer for text and image classification, and applied quantum self-attention and quantum recurrent neural networks to natural language processing tasks.
quotes: We re-implement a key representative set of these existing methods
to create a quantum hybrid transformer that works for text and image classification
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract states what the authors did.

assertions.value: The authors describe a quantum neural network as a variational algorithm with three steps: a quantum feature map encodes each classical data point, a variational model of parameterized gates is applied, and the circuit is measured with classical post-processing; for binary classification the class is given by the parity of the measured bit strings.
quotes: QNNs are a specific category within variational quantum algorithms, consisting of quantum circuits that incorporate gate operations parameterized for optimization
First, classical data is typically transformed into a quantum state using a quantum feature map to encode each data point
the probability of class 0 is associated with the probability of encountering even-parity bit strings, and likewise, for class 1, the probability of encountering odd-parity bit strings
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II defines the QNN setting the paper uses.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper gives the description without a derivation and cites other work for it.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum neural networks can represent a much larger state with exponentially fewer qubits than classical bits, potentially exponentially expanding their capacity for parallel processing, and that proposals allude to possible benefits such as accelerated training and enhanced processing speed.
quotes: represent a much larger state with exponentially fewer qubits than classical bits, potentially exponentially expanding their capacity for parallel processing
allude to possible benefits such as accelerated training and enhanced processing speed
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement with no evidence in this paper; the wording is hedged ('potentially', 'allude to').
assertions.reader_inference: No experiment in the paper measures a capacity or speed benefit.

assertions.value: The authors list three quantum data encodings: basis encoding, amplitude encoding (the probability amplitudes of a state represent the classical values) and angle encoding (rotation angles derived from the features), and state that angle encoding is the most commonly used in variational QML methods because of its efficiency.
assertions.anchor: Section III, PDF p.2 to p.3
quotes: Amplitude Encoding [18], where the probability amplitudes of a quantum state represent the values of classical data
The Angle Encoding method [19] uses one or more rotation operations, phase or otherwise, to encode each feature
is the most commonly used in variational QML methods due to its efficiency
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III defines the encodings the paper's models use.
assertions.reader_inference: The efficiency claim is stated without measurement here.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the QRNN the input at each step is embedded by angle encoding, with the RY rotation angle given by the inverse cosine of the input value.
quotes: is embedded into the quantum circuit via angle encoding Uin, with angles of the RY gates via the inverse cosine function
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III states the paper's own QRNN encoding.

assertions.value: The authors state that in fully quantum QRNNs the non-linear transformations of the recurrent blocks are replaced entirely by quantum circuits, called Quantum Recurrent Blocks, and that hybrid QRNNs typically use quantum circuits for acceleration.
quotes: In fully quantum QRNNs, the non-linear transformations of the recurrent blocks are replaced entirely by quantum circuits, making them Quantum Recurrent Blocks (QRBs).
Hybrid QRNNs typically use quantum circuits for acceleration [9].
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV.B defines the QRB the paper uses.

assertions.value: The authors state that QRBs are in general dense, allowing parameter compression, and that QRBs can potentially avoid gradient decay because of unitary RNN structures.
quotes: The QRBs in general are dense, thus allowing parameter compression.
The QRBs can also potentially avoid gradient decay as a result of unitary RNN structures [22].
assertions.certainty_reason: A hedged statement ('potentially') attributed to other work; not tested in this paper.

assertions.value: The paper lists three earlier QRNN proposals: one built from a quantum neuron with parameterized gates combined with amplitude amplification, a variational quantum recurrent neural network built from parameterized quantum circuits, and a quantum-enhanced RNN based on continuous variable quantum neural networks; it then focuses on a fourth model, reference [9].
quotes: [22] proposed one of the first QRNN models, consisting of a quantum neuron built using parameterized gates.
[23] constructed a variational quantum recurrent neural network using parameterized quantum circuits.
Here, we focus on one [9], which is composed of many quantum recurrent blocks shown in fig4.
assertions.certainty_reason: A literature summary of cited work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QRNN ansatz is built from layers of single-qubit and two-qubit gates, with an X-Z decomposition of three trainable rotation angles per single-qubit gate and two-qubit Rzz rotations for entanglement in a cyclic pattern; the Rzz gate is not intrinsic on most hardware but can be built from two CNOT gates around an RZ gate.
quotes: The X − Z decomposition was used for the single qubit gates in the circuit
Two-qubit Rzz rotation gates were used to entangle qubits
it can be implemented using two CNOT gates sandwiching an RZ gate
In fig.5, cyclic entanglement is used.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV.B states the paper's own QRNN circuit setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that the staggered QRNN needs less coherence time than the plain QRNN, and that they used the plain QRNN for its simple implementation in a statevector simulator, since the staggered QRNN needs dynamic circuits with a reset operation.
quotes: Thus the sQRNN needs less coherence time as compared to the pQRNN.
which we chose due to the simplicity of implementation in the statevector simulator, since sQRNN requires dynamic circuits
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV.B states which QRNN variant the paper ran and why.
assertions.reader_inference: The QRNN results therefore come from a statevector simulation of the plain architecture, not from hardware and not from the lower-coherence staggered form.

assertions.value: The authors state that they tested the QRNN, along with other models, on the MC and RP datasets and on the Amazon, Yelp and IMDB datasets, vectorized the text with TF-IDF, and trained a QRNN on each dataset for 200 epochs with a learning rate of 0.08.
quotes: we tested the QRNN model (along with others), on the Meaning Classification (MC) [26] and Relative Pronoun (RP) [27] datasets, as well as the the Amazon, Yelp, and IMDB datasets [28]
We trained a QRNN on each dataset for 200 epochs and used a learning rate of 0.08.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV.B states the paper's own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that each quantum self-attention layer has a quantum circuit part and a classical post-processing part: three parameterized circuits with the same ansatz and different parameters represent query, key and value.
quotes: QSAL consists of a quantum circuit part and a classical postprocessing part.
there are three main different parameterized quantum circuits, Uq, Uk, Uv which are employed to represent the query, key, and value components of the self-attention model

where α ̃s,j is the normalized gaussian projected self attention coefficient

quotes: One can be realized by a full quantum circuit without classical post-process [29].
However, this method requires plenty of qubits to be executed.
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited model and a stated limit of other work, not tested here.

papers.what_it_is: A simulation study of excited-state variational quantum eigensolvers (VQD against SSVQE, three optimizers, three ansatzes, qubit tapering) on LiH, plus a proposed folded-spectrum combination (FS-VQD, FS-SSVQE) tested on H4.

existing.note: The abstract claim holds as an iteration count, but the paper limits it: one setup (FS-VQE on LiH's first excited state, learning rate 0.07), and GD stopped at its 157th iteration still far from the target, so GD's count is the count at which its stopping rule fired, not a count to reach the same accuracy. Adam converged by its 134th iteration.
existing.value: The authors report that, in a folded-spectrum VQE run on the first excited state of LiH with one learning rate of 0.07 for all three optimizers, Adam converged by the 134th iteration to a final value 2.14×10−5 from the target, GD stopped at the 157th iteration with a final value 0.02247 short of the target, and QNG stopped at the 258th iteration with a final value 0.00429 from the target.
quotes: we maintain a consistent learning rate of 0.07 across all optimizers
GD’s cost function decays more and more slowly and stops at the 157th iteration.
The final value obtained using GD still falls 0.02247 short of the target
Finally, the cost function stops at the 258th iteration.
The final value obtained using QNG is 0.00429 away from the target.
converging by the 134th iteration
The final value is merely 2.14×10−5 from the target value.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one run of one molecule and one bond length.
existing.reader_inference: Each optimizer is shown from one run, with no repeat or seed spread. The stated counts differ by 23 between Adam and GD, and GD ended much farther from the target, so the ranking by iterations is not a ranking at equal accuracy.

assertions.value: The authors describe VQE as a hybrid quantum algorithm that gets the lowest eigenstate of a given Hamiltonian using a variational ansatz, with the loss function equal to the expectation value of the Hamiltonian, and state that the state with the minimum expectation value is approximately the ground state.
quotes: VQE is a hybrid quantum algorithm that gets the lowest eigenstate with a given Hamiltonian (H) using variational ansatz.
The state with optimal parameters θ∗, which has minimum ⟨H⟩, is approximately the ground state.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section I defines the method the paper uses.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum hardware with a lot of noise (gate error rates around 1 × 10−2) and a limited number of qubits (around 10 to 1000 physical qubits) is called Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices, and that the hardware error is still too large for quantum error correction.
quotes: the error is still too large for quantum error correction

The quantum hardware with lots of noise (gates’ error rate around 1 × 10−2) and a limited number of qubits (around 10 to 1000 physical qubits) is called Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices [17].
assertions.certainty_reason: Section I states the paper's own working definition of NISQ.

assertions.value: The authors describe VQD as adding the fidelity between the target state and lower-energy states to the loss function so the target is an excited state, and SSVQE as taking the sum of the Hamiltonian expectation values of orthogonal states as the loss function, so the ground and lower excited states come from a single parameter optimization.
quotes: adds the fidelity between target excited states and lower energy states to the loss function
takes the sum of different orthogonal states’ Hamiltonian expectation values as the loss function
obtaining both the ground and lower excited states within a single parameter optimization procedure is possible
assertions.certainty_reason: Section I defines the two methods compared.

assertions.value: The authors state that VQD uses a different parameterized unitary for each input state and optimizes the loss function of eq. (8) individually from the lowest state up to the k-th lowest state, with an overlap penalty that can be computed by a swap test (extra qubits and an ancilla) or by inversion of the unitary.
assertions.anchor: Section II.B.2, eq. (8), Fig. 2, PDF p.2 to p.3
quotes: VQD has different parameterized unitaries Uk(θk) for all input initial states {|ψk⟩}
The trick to acquire k lowest energy states using VQD is to optimize the loss function in eq. 8 individually from the lowest state to k th lowest state.
the swap test circuit can be utilized, requiring additional qubits to prepare another state and one ancilla qubit to obtain the overlap value
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II.B.2 defines the VQD procedure the paper runs.
assertions.reader_inference: VQD needs a separate optimization per state; the cost comparison with SSVQE counts that.

assertions.anchor: Section II.B.1, eqs. (5) to (7), PDF p.2
quotes: Original SSVQE requires two unitary transformations to search k-th excited state.
it’s hard to find a specific ansatz V (ϕ) that acts only on {|ψi⟩} and requires two optimization processes
which can acquire all excited states up to the k-th excited state through a single parameter optimization procedure

assertions.value: The authors state that the folded spectrum technique maps the target highly excited states to the ground state by changing the Hamiltonian to H prime equal to H minus omega, squared, where omega is an energy value close to the excited state's energy, and that FS-VQE is a normal VQE on the ground state of H prime.
quotes: The FS technique is a method to map the Hamiltonian’s target highly excited states to the ground state by changing the Hamiltonian
where ω is an arbitrary scaler energy value close to the excited state’s energy level. FS-VQE is a normal VQE to the ground state of H′.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II.B.3 defines the folded spectrum method used.

assertions.value: The authors state that FS-VQE was previously considered too costly because of the exponential growth of terms in the measured operator, and that the cited study uses a Pauli grouping technique that can significantly reduce the number of measurements and make FS-VQE a cost-efficient option.

employing a Pauli grouping technique, which can significantly reduce the number of required measurements and makes FS-VQE a cost-efficient option

assertions.value: The authors state that the UCCSD ansatz with fermionic single and double excitation operators requires many CNOT gates, which makes it challenging to implement on NISQ devices.

assertions.reader_inference: Table I gives accuracy 0.786 for two QT-NN rows with specificity 0.000 and sensitivity 1.000, which is the score of a model that predicts every flow as an attack. So the evaluated set holds about 78.6% attack flows and is not balanced between normal and attack. The paper does not give the subset size, the split, the test-set size or the positive rate. Under that rate, accuracies of 0.793 to 0.824 for the plain QNNs are close to the constant-prediction score.

assertions.value: The authors tabulate three plain variational QNNs with 8 qubits and no classical parameters: 6 layers (48 quantum parameters), 8 layers (64) and 10 layers (80), with accuracies of 0.799, 0.793 and 0.824, specificity of 0.066, 0.040 and 0.234 and sensitivity of 0.999, 0.998 and 0.986.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical simulation result from one study; one run per model.
assertions.reader_inference: Specificity near 0.04 to 0.07 with sensitivity near 1 means almost every normal flow is flagged as an attack. Specificity does not fall as depth rises across the three rows.

assertions.value: The authors tabulate five hybrid QNNs with 8 qubits and 18 classical parameters, with 2 to 10 layers: the 2-layer model (16 quantum parameters) has accuracy 0.926 and specificity 0.896, the 4-layer 0.933 and 0.861, the 6-layer 0.930 and 0.904, the 8-layer 0.948 and 0.838, and the 10-layer 0.944 and 0.920.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical simulation result from one study; one run per model.
assertions.reader_inference: Accuracy is 0.926 to 0.948 across all five depths, a spread of 0.022, and the SVM scores 0.924. HybridQNN-10L has the same qubit count and layer count as QNN-10L (accuracy 0.824) and differs by the 18-parameter classical head, which is the likeliest source of the gain. No model with that classical head and no quantum circuit is reported.
